questions.question: Which type of ulcer is characterised by multiple punched-out ulcers with undermined edges and necrotic bases on histopathological examination?

explanation.text: On histopathological examination, amoebic ulcers caused by Entamoeba histolytica present as multiple punched-out ulcers with undermined edges and necrotic bases ( flask-shaped ulcers ). The ulcers often have surrounding inflammation and contain trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica.
When Entamoeba histolytica goes to liver: It breaks the liver tissue into brown coloured pus known as Encovy sauce appearance TB ulcer (Option A): Transverse ulcer in direction.
**Typhoid ulcer (Option B):** Longitudinal ulcer in direction.

questions.question: A 60-year-old patient presents with severe diarrhoea and abdominal pain after completing a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics for a respiratory infection. Stool studies detect the presence of Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) toxin. A colonoscopy revealed diffuse yellowish plaques covering the colonic mucosa, as shown in the image. Which inflammatory cell type predominantly infiltrates the lamina propria and surface epithelium in this condition?

explanation.text: The given clinical condition suggests Pseudomembranous enterocolitis (PMEC). Pseudomembranous: On colonoscopy, diffuse yellowish plaques covering the colonic mucosa are seen. Enterocolitis: Inflammation of intestine Long term antibiotics alters the gut flora and makes person prone to C. difficile infection, which damages the intestine and forms pseudomembrane.

**Necrosis and damaged cells are always associated with neutrophilic infiltrations (Option C):** Patient presents with watery diarrhoea (rarely can present with bloody diarrhoea), Caused by 2 toxins of C. difficile: Toxin A and Toxin B On biopsy: Classical volcano like erruptions Drug of choice: Vancomycin ± Metronidazole New drug: Fidaxomicin

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents with chronic abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, and occasional blood in the stool. A colonoscopy reveals patchy erythema, oedema, and shallow ulcers with intervening normal mucosa in the terminal ileum and colon. The histopathological findings from the affected area are shown below. What histopathological features are observed in this patient's condition?

options.B: Smooth transition between ulcerated and adjacent normal mucosa
options.C: Absence of metaplastic changes in the epithelium
options.D: Uniform distribution of inflammation throughout the affected areas

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and biopsy findings showing noncaseating granulomas and skip lesions suggest Crohn’s disease. Noncaseating granulomas are round lesions with multinucleated giant cells within them.

questions.question: A 32-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and weight loss. A colonoscopy reveals findings consistent with Crohn's diseaseWhat histological features would you observe in this patient's biopsy?

options.D: Ulcers can extend beyond the mucosa

explanation.text: Crohn’s disease presents with transmural inflammation, which causes deep ulcers.

It is characterised by transmural inflammation and can affect the entire intestinal wall thickness, from the mucosa to the serosa, which can lead to fissures and fistulas. (Option A ruled out) Strictures or fibrosis are commonly seen in this condition (Option B ruled out) Ulcers are intially superficial and then goes deep extending to every layer of intestine. (Option C ruled out)

questions.question: Which statement is true regarding inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) pathogenesis?

options.A: NOD2 polymorphisms are closely associated with Crohn's disease in Asian populations.
options.B: ATG16L1 mutation promotes ATG16L1 degradation and enhances autophagy.
options.C: Dysbiosis is often established at disease presentation in IBD.

explanation.text: "Dysbiosis" refers to an imbalance in the gut microbiota characterised by shifts in microbial populations and reduced species diversity. This imbalance is commonly observed at the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Dysbiosis can lead to alterations in the gut environment, including increased inflammation and impaired barrier function, which may contribute to the progression of IBD. NOD2 polymorphisms are closely associated with Crohn's disease in Asian populations (Option A) NOD2 polymorphisms are closely associated with Crohn's disease but not with Crohn's disease in Asian populations.
**ATG16L1 mutation promotes ATG16L1 degradation and enhances autophagy (Option B):** The ATG16L1 mutation limits autophagy rather than enhancing it by promoting ATG16L1 degradation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease is true?

options.A: Ulcerative colitis is characterised by skip lesions, whereas Crohn’s disease typically presents with continuous inflammation.
options.B: Cobblestone appearance is a feature seen in ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease but is more commonly associated with Crohn's disease.
options.C: Ulcerative colitis typically begins in the rectum and extends proximally, whereas Crohn's disease can involve any part of the GI tract.
options.D: Fistulae, strictures, and abscesses are more commonly seen in ulcerative colitis than in Crohn's disease.

explanation.text: Features Ulcerative colitis Crohn’s disease Location Typically begins in the rectum and extends proximally affecting entire large and small intestines: Backwash ileitis Can involve any part of the GI tract: Primarily it starts most commonly from Ileum and then it can effect any part of GI tract in the forn of skip lesions.

Distribution Diffused continuous lesion Patchy, with skip lesions. (Option A) Gross appearance Mucosal erythema and granularity Broad-based ulcers with a continuous pattern Pseudopolyps Mucosal atrophy Smooth, continuous inflammation Transmural inflammation Aphthous ulcers Cobblestone appearance (Option B) Fistulae, strictures, abscesses Creeping fat (mesenteric fat wrapping) Complications Toxic megacolon Colonic dilation Mucosal bridges.
Strictures Fistulae Fissures (Option D)

questions.question: A 32-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with a 5-day history of non-bloody, watery diarrhea. He reports that he recently returned from a hiking trip in a rural area where he drank water from a nearby stream. On examination, he appears dehydrated but is otherwise stable. A stool sample was sent for analysis, which revealed the presence of oocysts. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's gastrointestinal symptoms?

explanation.text: Cryptosporidiosis is a significant cause of diarrhea worldwide. Cryptosporidium is known to cause non-bloody, watery diarrhea and is commonly associated with drinking contaminated water, particularly from untreated sources such as streams or lakes.

The presence of oocysts in the stool supports this diagnosis C. hominis and C. parvum usually presents with waterry diarrhea and many times the patient is immunocompromised like HIV+. Oocysts are present in stool and measures 4-6µm. Cold ZN stain or Kinyoun stain is used to see oocytes. On biopsy of intestine, Cryptosporidium is found along the brush border of epithelium.
**Microsporidium (Option B):** Rarely presents with oocysts in stool sample.
**Giardia lamblia (Option C):** Do not have oocysts.
**Entamoeba histolytica (Option D):** Do not have oocysts.

questions.question: A 20-year-old patient presents with a history of malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. A duodenal biopsy shows crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy, and CD8+ cells in the lamina propria. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanation.text: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by the ingestion of gluten in genetically predisposed individuals. The immune response leads to damage in the small intestine, causing malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. On histopathological examination, crypt hyperplasia, villous atrophy, and increased CD8+ T lymphocytes in the lamina propria are classic features of celiac disease.
Celiac disease Definition Autoimmune disorder triggered by ingesting gluten-containing foods in genetically susceptible individuals.

Synonym Gluten-sensitive enteropathy Celiac sprue Diagnosis Biopsy of the second part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum Serum markers Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG)-most sensitive Anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA)-most specific Histology Increased intraepithelial CD8+ T lymphocytes (intraepithelial lymphocytosis), Crypt hyperplasia (increased mitosis) Villous atrophy (reduced mucosal surface area, causing malabsorption) Inflammatory cells infiltration Environmental enteropathy (Option A) is a condition marked by chronic inflammation and structural changes in the small intestine.
It is commonly seen in individuals from regions with poor sanitation and hygiene.

**Whipple's disease (Option C):** is a rare bacterial infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei. It primarily affects the small intestine but can also involve other organs. The biopsy findings in Whipple's disease are different and typically show PAS-positive macrophages.

**Chronic pancreatitis (Option D):** is characterised by persistent inflammation and fibrosis of the pancreas, leading to impaired pancreatic function. It can cause malabsorption, but the biopsy would not show the characteristic findings of celiac disease, such as villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.

questions.question: What is the eye manifestation seen in HLA B27-positive patients with ulcerative colitis?

explanation.text: Uveitis Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) with possible extraintestinal manifestations. HLA-B27–positive patients have a higher risk of certain autoimmune complications, particularly in the eye. The most classic ocular manifestation is acute anterior uveitis. Features of uveitis in HLA-B27–associated IBD: Usually unilateral, sudden onset. Symptoms: eye pain, redness, photophobia, blurred vision.
Exam: ciliary flush, cells & flare in anterior chamber. Can be recurrent.

**Conjunctivitis (Option B):** It is more common in reactive arthritis (Reiter’s syndrome), not as strong an association with ulcerative colitis. Conjunctivitis involves superficial eye redness without the deep inflammation of uveitis.
**Scleritis (Option C):** Deep, boring eye pain; associated with systemic autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. It is less commonly seen in ulcerative colitis.
**Iridocyclitis (Option D):** refers to inflammation of the iris and ciliary body (a subset of anterior uveitis).

questions.question: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, is caused by mutations in which type of genes?

explanation.text: HNPCC / Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes. The most commonly affected genes are: MLH1 MSH2 MSH6 PMS2 Loss of these MMR proteins → failure to correct base-pairing errors → microsatellite instability (MSI) → increased risk of colorectal cancer (esp. right-sided) and extra-colonic cancers (endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract).

Lynch syndrome is associated with germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, leading to microsatellite instability (MSI). MSI is a hallmark of Lynch syndrome-associated tumours, including colorectal adenocarcinoma.
**APC (Option A):** tumor suppressor gene mutated in Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), not Lynch syndrome.
**MYC (Option C):** proto-oncogene involved in Burkitt lymphoma (t(8;14)), not colorectal cancer syndromes.
**TERT1 (Option D):** encodes telomerase reverse transcriptase; mutations linked to certain familial cancers but not HNPCC.

questions.question: In Barrett’s oesophagus, which of the following epithelial transformations occurs?

explanation.text: **Barrett's oesophagus is a complication of chronic GERD, characterised by intestinal metaplasia (Option B):** in the oesophageal squamous mucosa. It increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Occurs in 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Affects up to 2% of the general population. Most common in white males, typically between ages 40 and 60. Cancer Risk: Increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. The majority of oesophageal adenocarcinomas are associated with Barrett's oesophagus, but not all individuals with it will develop cancer. Recognised as red, velvety mucosa (Barrett's mucosa) extending upward from the gastroesophageal junction & alternating with pale squamous mucosa and light-brown gastric mucosa. Subclassified as long segment (≥3 cm) or short segment (<3 cm). Short-segment disease carries a lower cancer risk compared to long-segment disease. Intestinal-type metaplasia with goblet cells replacing squamous epithelium. Goblet cells are diagnostic of Barrett oesophagus and have distinct mucous vacuoles that stain blue with Alcian blue. This imparts the shape of a wine goblet to the remaining cytoplasm. Goblet cells are diagnostic, with pale blue mucous vacuoles resembling a wine goblet. Non-goblet columnar cells, like gastric-type foveolar cells, may also be present.
**Incorrect Options: Columnar to squamous (Option A):** occurs in squamous metaplasia (e.g., chronic irritation in bronchi of smokers), not Barrett’s.
**Transitional to squamous (Option C):** occurs in the bladder with chronic irritation (e.g., schistosomiasis).
**Cuboidal to columnar (Option D):** not typical in Barrett’s; cuboidal epithelium is seen in small ducts/glands, not in the oesophagus.

questions.question: Hepcidin acts on which of the following?

explanation.text: Ferroportin is an iron exporter protein found on the surface of cells, including enterocytes in the intestine. Hepcidin binds to ferroportin and induces its internalization and degradation. This leads to a decrease in iron export from the enterocyte into the plasma, thereby reducing iron absorption and availability.

Incorrect Options: Option A. Transferrin Transferrin is a protein that binds to iron in the plasma and facilitates its transport. Hepcidin does not directly bind to transferrin. Instead, hepcidin regulates iron levels by binding to ferroportin. Option C. Ferritin Ferritin is an intracellular protein that stores iron. Hepcidin does not directly bind to ferritin. Instead, hepcidin regulates iron levels by modulating the activity of ferroportin, which in turn affects iron release from ferritin. Option D. Divalent metal transporter 1 Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) is a transmembrane protein responsible for the uptake of iron from the lumen of the intestine into enterocytes. Hepcidin does not bind to DMT1. Its main target is ferroportin, which is involved in the release of iron from the enterocyte into the bloodstream.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Barrett's oesophagus?

explanation.text: The primary cellular change seen in Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia of squamous epithelium into intestinal/columnar epithelium.

Incorrect Options: Squamous Metaplasia (Option A) is the replacement of normal columnar epithelium with stratified squamous epithelium, typically due to chronic irritation (e.g., bronchial epithelium in smokers or the cervix). In Barrett's oesophagus, the reverse occurs, with squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium. Severe Dysplasia (Option B) is disordered cellular growth and a precancerous condition. In Barrett's oesophagus, dysplasia (low-grade or high-grade) may arise as a progression from intestinal metaplasia toward adenocarcinoma, but it is not a defining feature-rather, a complication. Cuboidal Metaplasia (Option D) is not a recognised feature of Barrett's oesophagus or any other oesophagal condition. Barrett's oesophagus is specifically defined by intestinal metaplasia, with goblet cells present within the columnar epithelium.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child was admitted to the hospital with a history of prolapsing rectal mass and painless rectal bleeding. The histopathological image of the mass is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and HPE image showing characteristic cystically dilated crypts & glands are suggestive of Juvenile polyp. Juvenile Polyps: Occurrence: Common in children under 5 years old; can be sporadic or syndromic. Size & Appearance: Typically less than 3 cm, pedunculated, smooth-surfaced, reddish with cystic spaces.

Histology: Dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris, mixed inflammatory infiltrates, and sometimes attenuated muscularis mucosae. Pathogenesis: Linked to mucosal hyperplasia; mutations in SMAD4 and BMPR1A (TGF-β pathway). Dysplasia: Rare in sporadic polyps but present in juvenile polyposis syndrome. Complications: Juvenile polyposis syndrome can lead to colonic adenocarcinoma (30-50% risk by age 45).

**Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (Option A):** is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract. While rectal polyps may occur in this syndrome, the histopathological image seen in this case is more indicative of juvenile polyps.
**Villous Adenoma (Option B):** are adenomatous polyps commonly seen in adults, characterised by finger-like projections with abundant mucin production.
**Tubular Adenoma (Option D):** are common adenomatous polyps found in adults, characterized by glandular structures with tubular architecture.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presented with a retroperitoneal mass. A biopsy of the lesion is shown in the image below. Molecular analysis revealed t(12;16). What is the most likely condition?

explanation.text: - Myxoid liposarcoma The presence of a retroperitoneal mass with the molecular finding of t(12;16) translocation & image showing abundant ground substance, with branching capillaries and few immature adipocytes, is highly suggestive of Myxoid liposarcoma. Liposarcoma, malignant tumours of adipose tissue, is the most common type of sarcoma in adults.

These tumours typically arise in the deep soft tissues of the proximal extremities and retroperitoneum, commonly affecting individuals in their sixth and seventh decades of life. Pathogenesis: The three subtypes of liposarcoma—well-differentiated, myxoid, and pleomorphic—have distinct genetic abnormalities: Well-differentiated liposarcomas exhibit amplifications in the chromosome region 12q13–q15, which includes the p53 inhibitor MDM2.

Myxoid liposarcomas are characterised by a fusion gene caused by a t(12;16) translocation, which arrests adipocyte differentiation, leading to uncontrolled proliferation of primitive cells. Pleomorphic liposarcomas display complex karyotypes without consistent genetic abnormalities. Histopathological findings: Well-differentiated liposarcomas are composed primarily of mature adipocytes with scattered atypical spindle cells.

Myxoid liposarcomas are characterised by a rich basophilic extracellular matrix, arborizing capillaries, and primitive cells at different stages of adipocyte differentiation, resembling fetal fat. Pleomorphic liposarcomas feature sheets of anaplastic cells with bizarre nuclei intermixed with varying numbers of immature adipocytes, called lipoblasts.
**Lipomas (Option B):** are benign tumours made up of mature adipose tissue. They are typically well-defined and do not show the cellular atypia or genetic abnormalities associated with liposarcomas.
**Spindle Lipoma (Option C):** is a benign variant of lipoma characterised by spindle-shaped cells within the fatty tissue. It lacks the genetic mutations seen in myxoid liposarcoma.

**Polymorphic Lipoma (Option D):** , also referred to as pleomorphic lipoma, is a benign lipomatous tumour made of mature adipose tissue containing various cell types. It does not exhibit the specific t(12;16) translocation found in myxoid liposarcoma.

questions.question: A 30-year-old female presents with chest pain, recurrent heartburn, and dysphagia. A barium swallow shows a bird beak sign. Which of the following statements is true regarding the condition in this patient?

options.C: Decreased release of NO and VIP in the distal esophagus

explanation.text: The clinical presentation & the bird beak sign on barium swallow suggests achalasia, a condition characterized by the inability of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax and an absence of peristalsis in the distal esophagus. It is caused by a decreased release of nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), which are essential for smooth muscle relaxation. This results in increased tone of the LES and impaired peristalsis.

Achalasia: Pathology: Incomplete LES relaxation/Increased LES tone/Aperistalsis of the esophagus Symptoms: Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), Difficulty in belching, Chest pain Primary Achalasia: It is caused by degeneration of nitric oxide-producing neurons that normally induce LES relaxation. Degeneration of the extraesophageal vagus nerve or dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus may occur.

Secondary Achalasia: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi infection) destroys the myenteric plexus, leading to peristalsis failure and esophageal dilation. Associated with conditions like: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy Infiltrative disorders (e.g., malignancy, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis ) Systemic sclerosis Dorsal motor nuclei lesions (post-polio) Down syndrome or Allgrove syndrome (achalasia, alacrima, ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency).

Some cases linked to HSV1 infection, immunoregulatory gene polymorphisms, Sjögren syndrome, or autoimmune thyroid disease, suggesting immune-mediated destruction of inhibitory esophageal neurons. Treatment: Laparoscopic myotomy Pneumatic balloon dilation Botulinum neurotoxin (Botox) injections to inhibit cholinergic neuron contraction.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the pathogenesis of Hirschsprung disease?

options.A: Failure of migration of neural crest cells

explanation.text: Hirschsprung disease arises when the migration of neural crest cells is arrested, causing a lack of ganglion cells (Option B ruled out) in the affected segment, leading to a lack of peristalsis in the affected bowel segment, causing functional obstruction and bowel dilation without inflammation or strictures (Option D ruled out). This leads to aganglionosis, preventing peristalsis and causing bowel dilation.

Morphology: Histopathological confirmation involves identifying the absence of ganglion cells, and acetylcholinesterase staining aids in diagnosis. The disease typically involves the rectum, with short-segment or long-segment Hirschsprung disease based on the extent of involvement. Clinical Features: Symptoms include failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, constipation, and bilious vomiting.

Complications such as enterocolitis, perforation, and peritonitis can occur. Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment is the primary treatment. Acquired Megacolon: Acquired Megacolon, seen in conditions like Chagas disease and ulcerative colitis, may share a similar pathophysiology with Hirschsprung disease, particularly in cases involving the loss of ganglion cells.
**Visceral myopathy (Option C):** refers to smooth muscle dysfunction, which can affect gastrointestinal motility but is not the cause of Hirschsprung disease.

questions.question: Match the following diseases with their respective gene mutation: 1. Familial adenomatous polyposis i. SMAD4 2. Juvenile polyposis ii. STK11 3. Tuberous sclerosis iii. APC gene 4. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome iv. TSC1

explanation.text: Below are some gene mutations and their associated manifestations: Genes mutation Manifestations MLH1, MSH2 Results in microsatellite instability Causes cluster of cancer: Colorectal, Endometrial, Ovarian, Pancreatic cancers Colon cancer develops at a young age, and it usually occurs on the right side.

SMAD4 and BMPR1 Juvenile polyposis syndrome STK11 Peutz-Jeghers syndrome APC gene Familial Adenomatous Polyposis(FAP), sporadic colon cancer, Gardner syndrome and Turcot syndrome MUTYH MUTYH-associated polyposis. TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) Tuberous sclerosis

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is correct? An arborizing pattern of smooth muscle Loss of heterozygosity in STK11 gene Multiple GI polyps Autosomal recessive inheritance Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigmental epithelium is seen

explanation.text: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome: Inheritance: Autosomal dominant. Age of Onset: Median age of 11 years. Key Features: Multiple GI hamartomatous polyps. Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation (dark macules on lips, buccal mucosa, palms, genitalia, and perianal region). Polyps are most common in the small intestine but may also occur in the stomach, colon, bladder, and lungs. Complications: Risk of intussusception, potentially fatal.

Increased cancer risk (lifetime risk ~40%), including cancers of the GI tract, testes, pancreas, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterus. Pathogenesis: It is caused by germline mutations in the STK11 gene, a tumour suppressor gene regulating cell polarization and growth. Somatic loss of the second STK11 gene copy in cancers. Morphology: Polyps are pedunculated and lobulated.

Histology shows an arborizing network of smooth muscle, connective tissue, lamina propria, and glands. Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigmental epithelium is not typically associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHTPE) is more commonly seen in other conditions, such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

questions.question: The cells lining the isthmus of gastric pits are:

explanation.text: The isthmus of the gastric pits contains stem cells, which are responsible for replenishing the various cell types in the gastric mucosa. These stem cells differentiate into different types of gastric cells, including parietal cells, chief cells, and mucous cells, as they migrate along the pit. Cell Type Location Function Stem cells Isthmus of gastric pits Regenerate the various types of gastric epithelial cells.

Parietal cells Fundus and body of the stomach It secretes hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factors that are important for digestion and vitamin B12 absorption. Chief cells Fundus and body of the stomach Secrete pepsinogen, which is converted to pepsin in the acidic environment, to aid in protein digestion.

Mucous cells Surface epithelium of the stomach lining and neck of gastric pits Secrete mucus to protect the stomach lining from the acidic environment and digestive enzymes. Endocrine cells (G cells) Antrum of the stomach Secrete gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion by parietal cells and gastric motility.
Enteroendocrine cells Throughout the gastric mucosa Secrete various hormones such as somatostatin, serotonin, and histamine to regulate gastric functions.
